To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the behavioral effects of electric shock on the behavior of ducklings imprinted to moving stimuli were similar to the effects observed in other species.

(a) electric shock, delivered in the presence of a moving stimulus, suppressed following behavior, (b) electric shock, presented in the absence of a moving stimulus but in the presence of an auditory stimulus, reduced the tendency for ducklings to choose the moving stimulus, and (c) the behavioral effects of electric shock were differentially determined by the schedule of shock presentation.
The schedule under which shock was presented to ducklings during and after imprint training was an important determinant of their subsequent behavior.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of punishment on the behavioral control of imprinting.
the behavioral effects of schedules of shock presentation during and after the formation of a social attachment in the Peking duckling.
the effects of aversive stimulation during the imprinting process.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the behavioral effects of shock in imprinted ducklings are not qualitatively different from those of other species.
the behavioral effects of punishment and avoidance schedules are not qualitatively different from those observed in other species of animals.
the effects of punishment and aversive stimulation are the same for imprinting and learning.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, in general, the behavioral effects of electric shock presentation are not different for imprinted and nonimprinted animals.
the behavioral control of the imprinted duckling can be modified by a variety of schedules of punishment and avoidance.
imprinting, like other forms of learning, can be influenced by a variety of schedules of reinforcement.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the schedule of shock delivery can be an important factor in determining the effects of shock on behavior.
, contrary to popular belief, aversive stimuli can be used to control the behavior of imprinted animals.
schedules of shock presentation are a critical determinant of the behavioral control of ducklings.
